businesses.pitch: Fields of solar panels that turn sunshine into electricity for thousands of homes.
businesses.earns: The power company pays you for every unit of electricity your panels make, often on a contract that lasts many years.
businesses.costs: Paying back the loan for the panels, land rent, cleaning, repairs, insurance and a small team of engineers.
businesses.risks: Cloudy summers, hailstorms, broken equipment, and the price of electricity falling when your contract ends.
businesses.tip: Lock in long contracts for your power, then keep every panel clean and working: sunshine is free, but only if you catch it.

cases.title: Fields, sheep and a big contract
cases.story: Your $3 million solar farm needs land and a buyer. Farmer Gwen will rent you her field if her sheep can keep grazing there. The power company offers to buy all your electricity at a fixed price for 15 years. What will you do?

options.text: Buy the cheapest panels from a website with no reviews
options.result: Half the panels crack in the first winter and the website has vanished. Replacing them costs far more than you saved.
options.lesson: For something that must last 25 years, quality beats the cheapest price.

options.text: Sign the 15-year deal so you know your income for years
options.result: With a buyer locked in, the bank lends to you at a lower rate. Sunny month or cloudy, every unit you make is already sold.
options.lesson: A long contract turns a gamble into a steady income you can plan around.

options.text: Raise the panels so Gwen's sheep can graze and keep the grass short
options.result: The sheep munch the grass between the rows, so you never pay for mowing. Gwen earns rent and keeps her flock.
options.lesson: The best partnerships help both sides: free mowing for you, rent and grass for Gwen.

options.text: Show the village your plans first and listen to their worries
options.result: Neighbours worry about the view, so you plant a tall hedge. Nobody objects, and the council approves your plans quickly.
options.lesson: Listening to neighbours early is cheaper than fighting them later.

options.text: Insure the farm against hail, storms and fire
options.result: You pay for cover every year and hope you never need it. If hail ever strikes, you won't have to pay for every broken panel yourself.
options.lesson: Insurance is a small, sure cost that protects you from a big, unlucky one.

cases.title: Hailstorm!
cases.story: A freak hailstorm cracks 3,000 of your panels in ten minutes. Your engineers want to start fixing them at once, but broken panels can still give an electric shock in daylight. The specialist repair crew is booked up unless you pay extra.

options.text: Get your own team fixing panels today: every sunny day counts
options.result: One engineer gets a painful shock from a broken panel (he is all right). Inspectors close the site for a month and fine you.
options.lesson: No sunny day is worth a hurt worker: make a site safe before anyone fixes it.

options.text: Fence off the broken rows and pay the specialist crew to come now
options.result: The crew arrives in two days, makes each row safe and swaps the panels. Within a fortnight you're back to full power, and nobody got hurt.
options.lesson: Safe and quick can go together: pay experts who know how to do dangerous work properly.

options.text: Order tougher, hail-resistant glass for the new panels
options.result: The new panels cost a bit more, but the next hailstorm bounces off them. Your repair bills shrink year after year.
options.lesson: When something breaks, fix it so it comes back stronger than before.

options.text: Use the quiet week to clean and test all the other panels
options.result: Your team finds 40 dusty or loose panels the hail never touched. Once they're fixed, the rest of the farm makes more power than before.
options.lesson: A bad day can be a good time to check everything else.

options.text: Leave the broken panels until next spring to save money
options.result: You save on repairs but lose a slice of your power every sunny day. By spring, the lost sales cost more than the repairs would have.
options.lesson: A cheap 'later' can cost more than paying to fix things now.

cases.title: A second farm, at half price?
cases.story: The city asks you to build a second solar farm. A new supplier offers panels at half price, but a news report says its factory makes children work. Your usual supplier costs more and checks its factories. You could also add giant batteries to store sunshine.

options.text: Take the half-price panels: their factory is not your problem
options.result: Reporters trace your panels to that factory. The city cancels your contract, people are furious, and you must replace every panel.
options.lesson: If children made it, it is your problem: what you buy is part of what you do.

options.text: Pay more for the checked supplier, and tell the city why
options.result: The city likes your honesty and agrees to a slightly higher price. The new farm opens on time, with panels made by fairly paid adults.
options.lesson: Doing the right thing, and explaining it openly, usually wins people over.

options.text: Add giant batteries to store midday sun for the evening
options.result: Power is worth most at teatime, when everyone gets home. Your batteries sell stored sunshine then, and your income grows steadier.
options.lesson: Selling the same thing at a better time can be worth as much as making more of it.

options.text: Send an inspector to visit the cheap supplier's factory
options.result: The inspector finds the report is true. You walk away, warn the city, and order from your usual supplier instead.
options.lesson: When a deal looks too cheap, go and see for yourself.

options.text: Say no to the city: one solar farm is plenty
options.result: Another company builds the farm instead and wins the city's next contract too. You missed a solid chance to grow.
options.lesson: Turning down a safe, good chance to grow has a cost too.

businesses.pitch: A fleet of quiet electric buses that carries thousands of people across the city.
businesses.earns: Passengers pay fares, and the city pays you to run its routes on time. Adverts on the sides of the buses bring in extra money.
businesses.costs: Drivers' pay, electricity for charging, repairs, the depot, insurance and paying back the loans for the buses.
businesses.risks: Breakdowns, batteries running low on freezing days, traffic jams, strikes, and losing the city's contract to a rival.
businesses.tip: A bus company runs on trust: buses on time, safe drivers and fares people can afford keep passengers coming back.

cases.title: Paying for the first buses
cases.story: Your first 10 electric buses cost $400,000 each. You could borrow from a bank, lease them (rent them by the month), or let the city pay part in return for cheaper fares for pupils and pensioners. You also need chargers and trained drivers.

options.text: Take the city deal: it pays a share, pupils and pensioners ride cheaper
options.result: The city pays a third of the cost. Cheap fares fill the buses with pupils and pensioners, and the city becomes your partner, not just a customer.
options.lesson: A partner who shares the cost also wants you to succeed.

options.text: Lease the buses so worn-out batteries are the maker's problem
options.result: You pay a steady amount each month instead of a fortune at once. When a battery wears out, the maker swaps it at no extra cost.
options.lesson: Leasing costs a little more over time but turns big surprises into steady bills.

options.text: Train every driver in smooth, safe driving before the first trip
options.result: Gentle starts and stops save battery power and make the ride comfy. Passengers notice, and your electricity bill drops.
options.lesson: Training your people well pays you back on every single trip.

options.text: Charge the buses overnight, when electricity is cheapest
options.result: Your depot charges every bus while the city sleeps, at the cheapest price of the day. Each morning the fleet rolls out full.
options.lesson: Small savings on something you buy every day add up to big money.

options.text: Borrow the lot and buy the biggest, flashiest buses on offer
options.result: The flashy buses look great but cost a fortune to repay. Half of them rumble round quiet routes nearly empty.
options.lesson: Buy what your passengers need, not what looks most impressive.

cases.title: The drivers' strike
cases.story: Your drivers say they'll strike (stop work) next Monday. They earn less than drivers at the rival bus company, and some shifts last 12 hours with hardly a break. Their leader, Priya, asks to meet you. Without drivers, not one bus leaves the depot.

options.text: Meet Priya and agree fair pay and proper breaks
options.result: It costs more each month, but the strike is called off. Rested drivers make fewer mistakes, and fewer of them leave for the rival.
options.lesson: Fair pay and proper rest keep your best people, and a happy team gives better service.

options.text: Show the drivers the real accounts so they see what you can afford
options.result: The drivers see the true numbers and agree to a pay rise in two steps. Trust grows on both sides.
options.lesson: Being open about money helps people agree on what is fair.

options.text: Rewrite the timetable so no shift is longer than 9 hours
options.result: You need a few more drivers, but nobody drives tired any more. Fewer bumps, fewer sick days and happier passengers.
options.lesson: Tired people make mistakes: good planning protects them and your passengers.

options.text: Hire stand-in drivers so the buses keep running
options.result: The stand-in drivers don't know the routes. Buses run late or get lost, and your own drivers feel betrayed.
options.lesson: Fighting your own team makes everyone lose, including your customers.

options.text: Promise a pay rise now, then quietly forget about it
options.result: The strike is called off, but when no pay rise comes, the drivers walk out for a whole month. Nobody believes your promises now.
options.lesson: A broken promise costs far more than the promise you didn't want to make.

cases.title: The school bus contract
cases.story: The city wants one company to run all its school buses for 10 years: a $9 million contract. A smooth-talking 'consultant' says that for a $100,000 'fee', he can make sure the council picks you. Bids (offers to do the job) close in a month.

options.text: Pay the consultant's 'fee': that's how big deals work
options.result: The 'fee' was a bribe. Investigators find the payment, you're banned from the contract, and the company is fined millions.
options.lesson: A secret payment to win a deal is a bribe, whatever name it's given.

options.text: Write the best honest bid: safe buses, trained drivers, a fair price
options.result: Your bid shows your safety record and your driver training. The council picks you because your plan is simply the best.
options.lesson: The safest way to win is to be the best, and to show it honestly.

options.text: Report the consultant's offer to the council's fraud team
options.result: The fraud team thanks you: he had tried the same trick on three companies. Councillors remember who spoke up.
options.lesson: Reporting a bribe protects you and keeps the contest fair for everyone.

options.text: Team up with a local bus firm to cover all the routes together
options.result: Together you have enough buses and drivers for every school. The council likes the local partnership, and you share the work and the profit.
options.lesson: A partner can help you win a job that is too big to do alone.

options.text: Bid a rock-bottom price to win, and worry about costs later
options.result: You win, but the price doesn't even cover the drivers' pay. Every school run loses money, for ten long years.
options.lesson: Winning a contract at a loss isn't winning.

businesses.pitch: A big indoor shopping centre with shops, cafés and a cinema under one roof.
businesses.earns: Shops pay you rent for their space, some also pay a share of their sales, and drivers pay to use the car park.
businesses.costs: Cleaning, security guards, heating and lighting, repairs, insurance, and paying back the loan for the building.
businesses.risks: Empty shops, online shopping pulling customers away, a newer centre nearby, and quiet months after Christmas.
businesses.tip: Your real customers are the shops: keep the centre busy, clean and safe, and good shops will queue to move in.

cases.title: Filling 80 empty shops
cases.story: Your shopping centre opens in six months with 80 empty shop spaces. A famous chain wants 20 of them at half rent. Local shop owners want small, cheaper spaces. The council will only give permission if there's a good bus stop.

options.text: Mix it up: a few big names to pull crowds, plus local shops
options.result: The big stores bring the crowds, and the local shops give people a reason to wander. Every space is rented by opening day.
options.lesson: A good mix spreads your risk: if one shop leaves, the others keep the centre busy.

options.text: Pay for the bus stop and a safe path into town
options.result: The council approves your plans, and buses drop shoppers at the front door. Families without cars can visit too.
options.lesson: Make it easy for everyone to reach you, and you get more customers and fewer objections.

options.text: Give the famous chain all 20 spaces at half rent
options.result: The chain fills a whole wing but pays half rent. When it closes stores two years later, the whole wing goes dark at once.
options.lesson: Relying on one big customer puts all your eggs in one basket.

options.text: Open a month early, before the fire safety checks are done
options.result: Inspectors find fire doors that won't close and shut the centre on its first busy weekend. The fine and the headlines cost far more than a month's rent.
options.lesson: Safety checks aren't a hurdle: they're what lets thousands of people shop safely.

options.text: Ask local people which shops they wish the town had
options.result: People ask for a bookshop, a climbing wall and a proper bakery. You find businesses for all three, and they're busy from day one.
options.lesson: Ask your customers what they want before you guess.

cases.title: Shoppers drifting away
cases.story: A shiny new centre opens across town, and more people shop online. Your visitors drop by a fifth, and three shops say they may leave when their rental contracts end. Your manager, Hamid, says: 'Give people something they can't get online.'

options.text: Turn empty spaces into things you can't do online: climbing, food, play
options.result: A climbing wall, a food hall and a soft-play centre open. Families spend whole afternoons here, and nearby shops get busier too.
options.lesson: When the world changes, change what you offer instead of hoping it changes back.

options.text: Help your shops offer 'order online, collect here'
options.result: Shoppers order on their phones and pick up by the entrance. Many grab a coffee and a few extra things while they're here.
options.lesson: If you can't beat a new habit, find a way to be part of it.

options.text: Cut rents a little for shops that stay five more years
options.result: You earn a bit less rent, but your shops stay put. A busy, full centre attracts new shops; an empty one scares them away.
options.lesson: A little less money for a lot more certainty can be a smart swap.

options.text: Cut cleaning and security to save money
options.result: Bins overflow and the toilets get grim. Shoppers notice at once and head to the shiny new centre instead.
options.lesson: When customers have a choice, never save money on the things they notice first.

options.text: Hold a giant sale weekend with music and prizes
options.result: The weekend is packed and fun! A month later, though, visitor numbers slide back down.
options.lesson: A party gives a quick boost; lasting change needs a lasting reason to come.

cases.title: Sign today, or lose the deal
cases.story: An investor, Mr Vance, offers $5 million for half your centre, far more than anyone else has offered. 'But you must sign today,' he says. 'Others are waiting.' The contract is 60 pages long, and your lawyer is away until Monday.

options.text: Sign today before he changes his mind
options.result: Hidden on page 52: if any shop pays its rent late, he can take the whole centre. You spend a fortune on lawyers to keep it.
options.lesson: 'Sign today' is pressure, not a reason: a good deal will still be there on Monday.

options.text: Say you'll decide after your lawyer has read every page
options.result: He gets cross, then stops calling. On Monday your lawyer finds a nasty trick on page 52. You've dodged it.
options.lesson: Real partners give you time to check. A rush is a warning sign.

options.text: Ask other investors what half the centre is really worth
options.result: Two investors value half your centre at about $3.5 million. His offer is far too high, which makes you wonder why.
options.lesson: When a price seems too good to be true, find out why before you say yes.

options.text: Check who Mr Vance really is and where his money comes from
options.result: His company was set up last month, and its address is an empty shop. Real investors don't hide who they are.
options.lesson: Before you take someone's money, find out whose money it really is.

options.text: Ask him to raise his offer to $6 million first
options.result: He agrees at once, which should worry you. Haggling over the price means nothing if the contract is a trap.
options.lesson: Don't argue about the price until you know what you're actually signing.

businesses.pitch: A giant, chilly building full of computers that store photos, games and websites.
businesses.earns: Companies rent space on your computers to run their apps, websites and online games, and they pay every month.
businesses.costs: Huge electricity bills, cooling to stop the computers overheating, security, engineers, and new machines every few years.
businesses.risks: Power cuts, overheating, cyber attacks, and big customers leaving if your service ever goes down.
businesses.tip: Your customers pay for 'always on': backups, spare power and strong security matter more than anything shiny.

cases.title: Building by the lake
cases.story: Your data centre will use as much power as a small town, and its computers must stay cool or they fail. You've found a site by a cold lake, next to a wind farm. Every customer wants one promise: never go offline.

options.text: Cool the computers with lake water and buy power from the wind farm
options.result: Cold lake water cools your machines for a fraction of the cost of air conditioning, and the wind farm sells you clean power at a fixed price.
options.lesson: Plan for the costs you'll pay every day, not just the cost of building.

options.text: Fit backup batteries and generators in case of a power cut
options.result: In your first winter, a storm cuts the town's power for six hours. Your batteries take over in a blink, and no customer notices.
options.lesson: When people pay you for 'always on', a backup plan is part of the product.

options.text: Train every worker to spot fake emails and lock every door
options.result: A month later, a worker spots a fake email pretending to be from you and reports it. The training has already paid for itself.
options.lesson: Most break-ins start with a trick on a person, so train your people, not just your machines.

options.text: Pipe the computers' spare heat to warm the town's swimming pool
options.result: Your machines make lots of heat anyway. Now it warms the town pool for free, and people call you a good neighbour.
options.lesson: One business's waste can be another's free treasure.

options.text: Buy second-hand computers to save money
options.result: The old machines break down every week. Customers' websites keep crashing, and two big customers leave for a rival.
options.lesson: When customers pay for reliability, unreliable equipment is the most expensive kind.

cases.title: Locked out by hackers
cases.story: At 3am your screens show a message: hackers have locked part of your system. An email demands $2 million in digital coins to unlock it and says, 'Tell no one.' Your backups are safe, but restoring them will take two days.

options.text: Pay the $2 million quietly so it all goes away
options.result: The hackers take the money, unlock only half, and ask for more. When customers learn you hid it, they're furious.
options.lesson: Paying criminals in secret rarely ends it: it marks you as someone who pays.

options.text: Restore your safe backups and tell customers honestly what happened
options.result: Two long days later, everything is back. Customers are cross about the wait but thank you for the truth, and almost all of them stay.
options.lesson: In a crisis, be quick, be honest, and lean on the backups you prepared earlier.

options.text: Call the police and a team of cyber-security experts at once
options.result: The experts find how the hackers got in (a weak password) and shut that door. The police add your case to a bigger investigation.
options.lesson: Calling in experts fast stops a small fire from becoming a big one.

options.text: Give every customer a month's discount to say sorry
options.result: It costs you a month of income, but customers feel looked after. Most sign up again when their contracts end.
options.lesson: Saying sorry with actions, not just words, helps people forgive.

options.text: Unplug everything, even the safe parts, until next week
options.result: Every customer goes offline, not just the hacked ones. A week of nothing costs far more than two days of careful repair.
options.lesson: Panic makes a problem bigger: switch off only what you must.

cases.title: A giant customer wants green
cases.story: A big company that makes AI (clever computer helpers that chat and answer questions) wants to rent half your data centre for 10 years. That doubles your power use, and the extra would come from gas. Its boss asks: 'Can you say you're 100% green?'

options.text: Say '100% green' in your adverts anyway: who will check?
options.result: A reporter checks your power bills. The adverts are banned, you're fined, and the AI company walks away embarrassed.
options.lesson: Greenwashing (pretending to be greener than you are) gets found out, and then nobody believes you.

options.text: Sign, and buy power from a new solar farm to cover the extra
options.result: A new solar farm agrees to sell you its power for 15 years. Your green claims are now true, and the AI company happily signs.
options.lesson: If customers want you greener, actually become greener, then tell them.

options.text: Tell them honestly what's green now and your plan to improve
options.result: The boss likes your honesty and signs a shorter deal while you go greener. Honest numbers make you a partner people trust.
options.lesson: Telling the truth about where you are today builds trust for tomorrow.

options.text: Make sure the contract says they pay for the extra electricity
options.result: When electricity prices jump the next winter, the AI company pays its own bill, just as the contract says. Your profit is safe.
options.lesson: Read who pays for what: one line in a contract can save you millions.

options.text: Rent them the whole centre and move your smaller customers out
options.result: Your smaller customers leave upset. Two years later the AI company builds its own centre, and you're left nearly empty.
options.lesson: One giant customer can leave you empty overnight, so never let one take everything.

businesses.pitch: A theme park full of roller coasters, water rides and shows for the whole family.
businesses.earns: Tickets at the gate, plus food, drinks, souvenirs, photos and hotel rooms. The summer holidays bring the biggest crowds.
businesses.costs: Hundreds of staff, ride safety checks and repairs, electricity, insurance, and building new rides to keep people coming back.
businesses.risks: Rainy summers, a ride breaking down, a safety scare in the news, and rival parks with newer, bigger rides.
businesses.tip: Safety is your real product: families only come back if they trust every ride, so check them daily and never cut corners.

cases.title: The star ride
cases.story: Your park needs a star ride. A trusted ride maker will build a new coaster for $3 million and train your staff. An online seller offers a used coaster from a closed park abroad for $800,000, 'no paperwork needed'. Opening day is in 8 months.

options.text: Buy the used coaster: no paperwork means no delays
options.result: Inspectors find rust and cracks in the track and refuse to let it open. Nobody else will buy it, and the money is gone.
options.lesson: On anything people ride, 'no paperwork' should make you walk away.

options.text: Order the new coaster from the trusted maker, with staff training
options.result: The coaster opens on time, every test passed. Your staff know every bolt, and on day one the queue stretches right round the lake.
options.lesson: Spending big makes sense when it buys safety and something people will love for years.

options.text: Hire an independent inspector to check every ride before opening
options.result: The inspector finds a loose bolt on the teacups before a single guest arrives. It's fixed in an hour.
options.lesson: A second pair of expert eyes catches what you're too busy to see.

options.text: Sell cheaper yearly passes to local families
options.result: Local families visit again and again, spending on food and souvenirs each time, and they bring friends from out of town.
options.lesson: Regular visitors are the steady heartbeat of a seasonal business.

options.text: Open without a star ride and add one in a few years
options.result: Visitors call the park 'nice but boring' online. Fewer come, so there's less money to build the star ride later.
options.lesson: First impressions are hard to change: open when you're truly ready to wow people.

cases.title: Stuck at the top
cases.story: Your big wheel stops for 40 minutes with families at the top. Everyone gets down safely, but a sensor that should have warned of the fault had been switched off. A video is already online, and reporters are calling.

options.text: Call it a 'planned stop' and reopen the wheel tomorrow
options.result: Engineers' notes show the sensor was off. The truth comes out, the park is closed for a month and fined heavily.
options.lesson: Hiding a safety problem turns a bad day into a disaster.

options.text: Close the wheel, find out why the sensor was off, and tell the public
options.result: Checks show a worker switched it off to stop false alarms. You fix the sensor and the rules, and tell everyone exactly what changed.
options.lesson: When something goes wrong, fix the cause and be open about it.

options.text: Phone every family who was stuck, say sorry and invite them back
options.result: Most families are touched that the boss called. Several post online that the staff were calm and kind while they waited.
options.lesson: A real apology from the top shows people they matter.

options.text: Teach every ride worker why each safety system matters
options.result: Staff learn that alarms are guardians, not nuisances. Next summer they spot two small faults early and fix them before the gates open.
options.lesson: Rules work best when people understand why they exist.

options.text: Blame the worker in public and sack him
options.result: Other staff start hiding mistakes in case they're next. The real problem, a system that let anyone switch sensors off, is still there.
options.lesson: Blaming one person hides the real problem; fixing the system solves it.

cases.title: Dragons and a second park
cases.story: A film studio wants to build a ride based on its hit dragon film at your park. It will pay half the $4 million cost but wants a fifth of all your ticket money for 10 years. Another city also asks you to open a second park there.

options.text: Agree, but share only the dragon ride's money, not the whole park's
options.result: The studio agrees after some tough talks. The dragon ride becomes the park's favourite, and the rest of your ticket money stays yours.
options.lesson: Don't just accept a deal: negotiate the part that matters most to you.

options.text: Ask a ride expert to check the studio's design before signing
options.result: The expert spots that the queue has no shade. The studio adds a cool dragon cave to queue in, which children love.
options.lesson: Listening to experts before you sign is cheaper than fixing things after.

options.text: Sell dragon toys and costumes in the shop by the ride
options.result: Children love the dragon wings. The shop by the ride sells out every Saturday.
options.lesson: A popular attraction can sell much more than tickets.

options.text: Study the other city for a year before deciding
options.result: You learn its summers are short but its school holidays are long. A smaller, indoor park there looks like a much better plan.
options.lesson: Research before you expand: what works in one city may flop in the next.

options.text: Open a second park in the other city straight away
options.result: Building two parks at once stretches your money and your best managers. The new park opens late and over budget.
options.lesson: Get one thing working brilliantly before you copy it somewhere else.

businesses.pitch: A professional football club with a stadium, a team of players and thousands of fans.
businesses.earns: Match tickets, TV money, shirt sponsors, selling kits, and sometimes selling a player to a bigger club for a big fee.
businesses.costs: Players' wages (the biggest cost by far), coaches, the stadium, travel, the youth academy, and fees to buy new players.
businesses.risks: A losing run, star players getting injured or leaving, dropping down a league, and spending money the club hasn't got.
businesses.tip: Never spend next year's money on this year's players. Clubs that grow their own young talent stay strong for years.

cases.title: Taking over the club
cases.story: You've bought a club in the second division, and the fans want promotion now. Coach Amara says the youth academy is full of talent but needs $2 million. An agent offers three star players, paid for with a big loan.

options.text: Borrow big and buy the three star players now
options.result: The stars win a few matches, but their wages and the loan swallow everything. After one season you must sell them at a loss.
options.lesson: Borrowing to chase a quick win can leave you with the bill and no win.

options.text: Invest in Amara's youth academy and coaches
options.result: Three years later, two of your own teenagers star in the first team, and a big club offers $8 million for one of them.
options.lesson: Growing your own talent is slower, but it costs less and it lasts.

options.text: Meet the fans' groups and share your honest plan
options.result: Fans hear that promotion may take three seasons, not one. Most respect the honesty, and season tickets still sell out.
options.lesson: Honest expectations stop disappointment before it starts.

options.text: Sign one experienced player on a fair wage to guide the young ones
options.result: Your new veteran defender keeps the team calm and coaches the youngsters during matches. Results get steadier.
options.lesson: One wise, experienced person can lift a whole young team.

options.text: Raise ticket prices by half to pay for everything
options.result: Thousands of loyal fans can't afford to come. The stadium echoes, and the players miss the roar of a full home crowd.
options.lesson: Price out your most loyal customers and you lose more than money.

cases.title: The star wants to leave
cases.story: Your top scorer, Kofi, says he wants to join a bigger club, and a rich club offers $15 million for him. He has two years left on his contract, and the fans adore him. Your coach says losing him mid-season could hurt.

options.text: Sit down with Kofi to hear what he really wants
options.result: Kofi admits he dreams of playing in the top league, not of more money. You agree a plan that keeps everything friendly.
options.lesson: Ask what people really want before you decide what to offer them.

options.text: Sell him at the end of the season, and spend the fee on young talent
options.result: Kofi's goals win you plenty of matches this season, then he leaves with the fans' thanks. The $15 million builds a team of hungry young players.
options.lesson: When you can't keep a star, plan the exit so it makes the team stronger.

options.text: Tell reporters he's injured, so other clubs stop bidding
options.result: Kofi scores twice on Saturday, so everyone knows you lied. A sponsor pulls out, and fans stop trusting anything the club says.
options.lesson: Lie to the public once, and every word you say afterwards is worth less.

options.text: Refuse to sell and leave him out of the team until he gives in
options.result: An unhappy Kofi sits in the stands, the team loses without him, and his value drops. Everybody loses.
options.lesson: Forcing someone to stay who wants to leave rarely works out for anyone.

options.text: Ask for a share of the fee if his new club ever sells him on
options.result: The rich club agrees to pay you a tenth of any future fee. Four years later Kofi moves again, and a surprise cheque arrives.
options.lesson: One clever extra line in a deal can keep paying you for years.

cases.title: A bigger stadium
cases.story: Your stadium is full every match, and a bigger one would cost $30 million. You could sell shares (small pieces of the club) to fans, ask the city to help, or let a company put its name on the stadium for $1 million a year.

options.text: Sell shares to fans so they own part of their club
options.result: Twenty thousand fans buy shares and raise millions. Now they feel like owners of the club, because they are.
options.lesson: When customers become owners, they become your strongest supporters.

options.text: Ask the city to share the cost if schools can use it too
options.result: Schools use the pitches on weekdays, and the city pays a third of the cost. The whole town feels the stadium is theirs.
options.lesson: A project that helps the whole community finds more people willing to pay for it.

options.text: Let a company name the stadium for $1 million a year
options.result: Fans grumble about the new name at first, but the money pays for a new roof over the stands. Soon everyone uses the name.
options.lesson: Selling a name can pay for a dream, if the partner fits your club.

options.text: Borrow the whole $30 million and build the biggest stadium around
options.result: The giant stadium is half empty on cold Tuesday nights, and the loan payments drain the money meant for players.
options.lesson: Build for the crowds you really have, not the crowds you dream of.

options.text: Squeeze 2,000 extra seats into the aisles without asking the safety officer
options.result: The safety officer spots it at the first match and closes the stand. You refund thousands of tickets and pay a big fine.
options.lesson: In a crowd of thousands, safety rules aren't red tape: they're how everyone gets home safely.

businesses.pitch: A busy harbour where giant ships unload thousands of containers full of goods.
businesses.earns: Shipping companies pay a fee for every container you lift on or off their ships, and for storing containers on the dock.
businesses.costs: Giant cranes and their repairs, dockworkers' wages, power, keeping the harbour deep enough for big ships, and security.
businesses.risks: Storms that close the harbour, strikes, a broken crane, shipping lines moving to a rival port, and pollution fines.
businesses.tip: Ships hate waiting: a port that turns ships around quickly and safely wins the shipping lines' business for years.

cases.title: Cranes, seals and the union
cases.story: Your new dock needs giant cranes and a deeper harbour, but digging could disturb seals that live nearby. One crane maker is cheap; another has a strong safety record. The dockworkers' union (a group that speaks for workers) wants a say in safety.

options.text: Ask wildlife experts, and dig only when seal pups aren't being born
options.result: The digging takes a few weeks longer, but the seals stay and the council approves your plans. Visitors even come to watch them.
options.lesson: Listening to experts can protect nature and your permission to build at the same time.

options.text: Buy the cranes with the strong safety record
options.result: The cranes cost more, but they rarely break down and come with training. Ships unload faster, so more of them choose your port.
options.lesson: For machines that lift 30 tonnes over people's heads, the safest choice is also the smart one.

options.text: Set up a safety team with the union from day one
options.result: Workers point out a blind spot where lorries and people cross. You build a footbridge before anyone gets hurt.
options.lesson: The people doing the job often spot the dangers first, so ask them.

options.text: Insure the cranes and the containers against storms
options.result: The cover costs a bit every year. When a winter storm topples a stack of empty containers, the insurer pays for the damage.
options.lesson: When one bad night could cost millions, insurance is part of good planning.

options.text: Offer shipping lines half price for a year to win them over
options.result: Ships arrive, but you lose money on every container. When the year ends and prices rise, half of them sail off to the next cheap port.
options.lesson: Customers won with a giant discount often leave when the discount does.

cases.title: Clean air rules
cases.story: A new city rule says ships must switch off their smoky engines while docked, or the port is fined. You'd need shore power: plugs that let ships use the city's electricity. Meanwhile a waste firm offers to take ships' oily waste for half price, 'no paperwork'.

options.text: Use the half-price waste firm: the waste is their problem now
options.result: The firm dumps the oily waste in a river at night. It's traced back to your port, and the clean-up and fines cost millions.
options.lesson: If a deal is cheap because it skips the rules, nature pays first, and then you do.

options.text: Install shore power so ships can plug in instead of running engines
options.result: The harbour air gets cleaner, neighbours notice, and shipping lines with greener ships pick your port. No fines either.
options.lesson: Meeting a new rule early can turn it into an advantage over slower rivals.

options.text: Charge ships a small fee to plug in, to pay back the cost
options.result: Ships pay a fair fee to plug in, and the greener shipping lines don't mind at all. The plugs pay for themselves within a few years.
options.lesson: A fair fee for a useful new service helps pay for the investment.

options.text: Ask the city to help pay, since clean air helps everyone
options.result: The city pays a quarter of the cost from its clean-air fund. Asking politely, with good reasons, worked.
options.lesson: When your project helps the whole city, it's fair to ask the city to help too.

options.text: Pay the fines for now: it's cheaper than plugs this year
options.result: The fines grow every year, and local families campaign against the 'dirty port'. In the end you still have to buy the plugs.
options.lesson: Paying to keep doing the wrong thing only delays what you'll have to do anyway.

cases.title: The giant shipping line
cases.story: One of the world's biggest shipping lines wants to make your port its main base, bringing 40% more ships. In return it wants the best berths (parking spots for ships) and a big discount for 10 years. Your smaller customers fear being pushed aside.

options.text: Agree, but keep some berths for the smaller lines too
options.result: The giant brings its ships, and your smaller customers keep their spots. If it ever leaves, your port won't be left empty.
options.lesson: Grow with a big customer, but never let one customer own your whole business.

options.text: Build a rail link so containers leave by train, not lorry
options.result: One train carries as many containers as dozens of lorries. The roads are quieter, the air is cleaner and goods move faster.
options.lesson: Think about the whole journey, not just your part, and you become hard to beat.

options.text: Hire and train 100 extra local dockworkers
options.result: Local families get good jobs, and the extra ships are unloaded on time. The town is proud of its growing port.
options.lesson: Growth goes better when the community grows with you.

options.text: Ask for a price check together every three years
options.result: The shipping line agrees to review the price with you every three years. Neither side gets stuck with a bad deal for a decade.
options.lesson: Long deals need a way to adjust, because the world keeps changing.

options.text: Give them everything they ask: all the best berths and the discount
options.result: Your smaller customers leave in a huff. Then the giant demands even bigger discounts, knowing you can't afford to lose it.
options.lesson: If one customer is your whole business, they hold all the power.

businesses.pitch: A gleaming tower of offices and flats that rises above the whole city.
businesses.earns: Companies rent offices and families rent flats, all paying rent every month. A rooftop restaurant pays rent too.
businesses.costs: Lifts, cleaning, security, heating and cooling, window washing, insurance, and paying back the huge building loan.
businesses.risks: Empty floors when companies move out, building delays, rising loan payments, and costly repairs to lifts and windows.
businesses.tip: Sign up good tenants before you finish building, then keep them happy: a full tower earns every month, an empty one just costs.

cases.title: Paying for a 60-storey tower
cases.story: Your 60-storey tower will cost far more than you have. The bank will lend more cheaply if some floors are rented before building starts. Your architect, Leila, suggests thick insulation (padding that keeps heat in) and solar glass: dearer now, but lower energy bills for decades.

options.text: Rent out the top floors early to a big firm at a fair price
options.result: A design company signs for the top ten floors before a brick is laid. Seeing rent already promised, the bank lends at a lower rate.
options.lesson: Promised income makes lenders trust you, and trust makes borrowing cheaper.

options.text: Follow Leila's design: thick insulation and solar glass
options.result: The tower costs more to build, but heating and cooling bills are a third lower for decades. Tenants love the low bills.
options.lesson: Paying a little more now can save a lot every year for decades.

options.text: Have experts test the ground before you start digging
options.result: The experts find soft clay under one corner. Deeper foundations cost a little extra but keep your tower standing straight for a century.
options.lesson: The most important part of a tall building is the part nobody sees.

options.text: Add a public garden and playground at the foot of the tower
options.result: Office workers eat lunch there, and families play after school. The council loves it, and tenants say it's one reason they chose you.
options.lesson: A building that gives something back to its street is easier to love, and to rent.

options.text: Hire the cheapest builder, who promises to finish in half the time
options.result: Half the time turns into twice the time: the builder keeps running out of workers. Every month of delay means no rent.
options.lesson: A promise that sounds too fast and too cheap usually turns out to be neither.

cases.title: Behind schedule
cases.story: Your tower is four months behind because a steel delivery came late. Companies waiting to move in are getting impatient, and every month of delay costs about $400,000 in lost rent. The builder says: 'Skip the sprinklers on the top floors for now, and we'll add them later.'

options.text: Skip the sprinklers for now to catch up
options.result: The fire inspector refuses to sign off the tower. Fitting sprinklers late means ripping out new ceilings: more delay, more cost.
options.lesson: Fire safety is never something to add 'later': it's what lets people live and work safely.

options.text: Pay for an extra shift of workers, keeping every safety check
options.result: An evening shift works under bright lights with full safety checks. You win back three months, and the tower opens almost on time.
options.lesson: When you're behind, add effort, not risk.

options.text: Tell the waiting companies honestly and give them a month rent-free
options.result: They're disappointed but grateful for the honesty. Not one cancels, and several promise to stay longer.
options.lesson: Bad news told early and honestly keeps trust; bad news hidden destroys it.

options.text: Find a second steel supplier so one late delivery can't stop you
options.result: When the first supplier is late again, the second one delivers. It takes a little extra effort, but you're never stuck.
options.lesson: Never depend on just one supplier for something you can't build without.

options.text: Blame the steel company in the newspapers
options.result: The steel company hits back with its own story, and the papers write about the row instead of your tower. Nothing gets built faster.
options.lesson: Arguing in public rarely fixes a problem; working on it does.

cases.title: A famous tenant's demands
cases.story: A tech company wants 30 floors as its headquarters for 15 years. It asks for the first year rent-free, its name in giant letters on top, and a promise you'll never rent to its rivals. It would fill half your tower.

options.text: Agree to the name, but swap the free year for three free months
options.result: After some tough talks they agree. Half your tower is rented for 15 years, and their name on top makes it famous.
options.lesson: Good deals come from trading: give what costs you little, keep what matters most.

options.text: Check its accounts to make sure it can pay for 15 years
options.result: Its accounts are strong and growing. Now you can sign knowing the rent is safe.
options.lesson: A long contract is only as good as the company that signs it.

options.text: Turn the empty top floor into a viewing deck with tickets
options.result: Tourists queue to see the whole city from up high. The ticket money pays for all the window cleaning, and more.
options.lesson: Look for hidden value in what you already own.

options.text: Promise never to rent to any of its rivals
options.result: Two rival firms ask to rent your empty floors, and you have to say no. Those floors stay empty for a whole year.
options.lesson: Never promise away future customers without working out the cost.

businesses.pitch: An airline whose planes fly holidaymakers and business travellers around the world.
businesses.earns: Ticket sales, plus extra for bags, roomier seats and meals. Carrying parcels in the hold under the seats earns money too.
businesses.costs: Jet fuel (huge, and its price jumps up and down), planes, pilots and crew, safety checks, airport fees and insurance.
businesses.risks: Fuel prices jumping, a quiet summer, storms and strikes cancelling flights, and rivals cutting prices to win your passengers.
businesses.tip: Keep your planes full and flying, never skimp on safety, and protect yourself against fuel prices before they jump.

cases.title: Ten planes and a plan
cases.story: To start your airline you need 10 planes. Buying them would use up all your money. Leasing (renting them by the year) costs more over time but keeps cash spare. You must also choose your first routes and hire pilots.

options.text: Lease the planes and keep a cash cushion for bad months
options.result: When a quiet winter comes, you hand two planes back early and live off your cushion. A rival that bought every plane struggles to pay its loans.
options.lesson: In a business with big ups and downs, spare cash is what gets you through the downs.

options.text: Hire experienced pilots and make it safe for anyone to report a problem
options.result: A young engineer reports a worn part the checklist missed. Because nobody is punished for speaking up, problems get fixed early.
options.lesson: The safest companies make it easy for anyone to say 'something isn't right'.

options.text: Start with three busy routes where you know people want to fly
options.result: Your planes fly full from the start between three busy cities. The profit from those routes pays for the next ones.
options.lesson: Prove your idea where demand is strong before you spread out.

options.text: Fix next year's fuel price now with a 'hedge' (a price deal)
options.result: When fuel prices jump in spring, you're still paying the agreed price. A hedge works like insurance against expensive fuel.
options.lesson: When one big cost can swing wildly, fixing its price ahead of time lets you plan.

options.text: Squeeze in extra seats so every flight carries more people
options.result: Your planes carry more people, but knees are squashed and reviews are cruel. Many passengers choose another airline next time.
options.lesson: Saving money at your customers' comfort can cost you their return.

cases.title: Fuel prices take off
cases.story: Jet fuel prices jump by half in a month, and your profit vanishes. One manager suggests saving money by doing the planes' safety checks less often. A rival airline has already raised its fares.

options.text: Do safety checks less often until fuel gets cheaper
options.result: The air safety authority finds the missed checks and grounds your planes for two weeks. The fines and refunds are enormous.
options.lesson: Safety checks are never the place to save money: not in a crisis, not ever.

options.text: Fly your most fuel-saving planes and cut the emptiest flights
options.result: Your newest planes burn far less fuel. Passengers from the cut flights move onto fuller ones, and you're making money again.
options.lesson: In a squeeze, cut waste first, not safety and not service.

options.text: Add a small fuel charge to tickets, and explain why clearly
options.result: Most passengers understand, since every airline is doing the same. Being clear about it stops angry surprises at the checkout.
options.lesson: Explain a price rise honestly and people are far more likely to accept it.

options.text: Teach pilots fuel-saving habits, like taxiing on one engine
options.result: Small habits, like rolling to the runway on one engine, save tonnes of fuel every week. The pilots are proud of their savings.
options.lesson: Lots of small savings, made every day, can beat one big cut.

options.text: Cut the cabin crew's pay without warning
options.result: The crew are furious and strike in the busiest week of summer. You lose far more than you saved.
options.lesson: Cutting pay without talking first turns a money problem into a people problem.

cases.title: A rival wants to merge
cases.story: A smaller rival airline is struggling and asks to join with yours (a merger). You'd get its planes and routes. A friend who works there whispers: 'It's secret. Buy its shares (small pieces of the company) now, before the price jumps!'

options.text: Buy the rival's shares now, before the news comes out
options.result: Using secret information to buy shares is called insider dealing, and it's against the law. Investigators spot your trade and fine you millions.
options.lesson: Secret share tips aren't lucky breaks: using them breaks the law.

options.text: Merge after experts check its planes, debts and safety records
options.result: The checks find two planes needing new engines, so you agree a lower price. The joined-up airline flies to twice as many places.
options.lesson: Check before you buy: what you find can change the price, or the whole deal.

options.text: Promise the rival's staff fair jobs in the new airline
options.result: The rival's crews stay calm and keep flying while the two airlines join. Passengers notice nothing but the new routes.
options.lesson: People do their best work when they know they'll be treated fairly.

options.text: Tell your friend you won't use the tip, and tell your lawyer
options.result: Your lawyer says you did exactly the right thing. Months later, people who traded on the rumour are caught, and your name stays clean.
options.lesson: When you hear a secret you shouldn't use, say no and tell someone who can protect you.

options.text: Announce the merger online before it's agreed
options.result: The deal isn't finished, and your post causes chaos. The rival's boss is furious, and the deal nearly falls apart.
options.lesson: Keep a deal quiet until it's signed and announced properly.

businesses.pitch: A rocket company that flies paying passengers to the edge of space to see Earth.
businesses.earns: Each seat on a flight sells for hundreds of thousands of dollars, plus money from sponsors, films and science experiments.
businesses.costs: Building and testing rockets, fuel, a launch site, top engineers, training passengers, and very expensive insurance.
businesses.risks: A failed test can delay flights for months, investors may lose patience, and one safety mistake could end the company.
businesses.tip: In space, safety is everything: test, test and test again, and let engineers, not deadlines, decide when to fly.

cases.title: Ready for lift-off?
cases.story: Your first rocket is built, and 600 people have paid deposits (money up front) for $250,000 seats. Investors want the first passenger flight in three months. Your chief engineer, Dr Okafor, wants six test flights with nobody on board first, which will take a year.

options.text: Do all six test flights with nobody on board, then fly passengers
options.result: Test four finds a valve that sticks in the cold. It's fixed long before any passenger climbs aboard, and later flights go smoothly.
options.lesson: Testing is not a delay: it's how you find problems while nobody is in danger.

options.text: Fly passengers in three months to keep the investors happy
options.result: The space safety authority refuses a licence without proper tests. The rushed date passes, you refund angry customers, and investors lose trust anyway.
options.lesson: Let engineers, not deadlines, decide when it's safe to fly.

options.text: Insure the rockets and the launch site
options.result: It's expensive, because space is risky. But if a test rocket is ever lost, you can build another without going bust.
options.lesson: The riskier the business, the more insurance matters.

options.text: Write to all 600 customers explaining the safety plan and the new date
options.result: Only a handful ask for refunds. Most write back that they'd rather wait and be safe, and some even send the engineers biscuits.
options.lesson: Customers trust a company that tells them the truth, even about a delay.

options.text: Spend the deposits on a giant advertising campaign
options.result: Everyone has heard of you, but the money meant for rockets is gone. When a test needs fixing, there's no cash left to pay for it.
options.lesson: Customers' deposits are a promise to keep, not spending money.

cases.title: A test goes wrong
cases.story: Your fifth test rocket, with nobody on board, has an engine fault and splashes into the sea. No one is hurt, but passenger flights must wait six months. Tomorrow you meet investors who have put in $30 million. A manager says: 'Just tell them all five tests went perfectly.'

options.text: Tell the investors all five tests went perfectly
options.result: A video of the splash is online by lunchtime. Investors feel tricked, some take you to court, and the news says you misled them.
options.lesson: Dressing up bad numbers to impress investors is lying, and the truth always comes out.

options.text: Show investors exactly what went wrong and how you'll fix it
options.result: The investors are disappointed, but your honest, careful plan impresses them. Most stay, and one even invests more.
options.lesson: Investors can live with bad news; what they can't live with is being misled.

options.text: Let the engineers find the cause, however long it takes
options.result: The cause is a tiny crack in a fuel pipe. The fix takes four months, and the next three tests go perfectly.
options.lesson: Fix the cause, not just the symptoms, before you try again.

options.text: Offer waiting customers a refund or a longer flight later
options.result: A few take refunds, but most choose the longer flight. Your waiting list hardly shrinks.
options.lesson: When you make customers wait, give them a fair choice and most will stay.

options.text: Sack the engineers who built the faulty engine
options.result: Your best engineers leave, taking the knowledge you need most. The fix takes even longer, and nobody dares report problems now.
options.lesson: Punishing honest failure teaches people to hide the next one.

cases.title: Shares or satellites?
cases.story: Big banks say you could sell shares (small pieces of your company) on the stock market and raise $20 million. The government also offers a 5-year contract to carry science satellites into space: less exciting than tourists, but paid every month.

options.text: Take the satellite contract for steady money between tourist flights
options.result: Satellites pay the bills even when tourist seats sell slowly. Your rockets fly more often, so your team learns and improves faster.
options.lesson: A steady customer alongside an exciting one keeps the lights on.

options.text: Sell shares, with an honest booklet explaining the risks
options.result: Some investors decide space is too risky for them, which is fair. Those who buy know the risks, and you raise $15 million.
options.lesson: Investors who know the risks up front stay calm when things get bumpy.

options.text: Ask the engineers if the rockets can safely fly that often
options.result: The engineers say yes, if they get a second launch crew. You hire one, and both kinds of flight run smoothly.
options.lesson: Before you promise more, ask the people who'll have to deliver it.

options.text: Let a fizzy-drink company paint its logo on the rocket
options.result: The sponsor money is nice for a few months, and the bright rocket looks great in photos. Then the deal ends.
options.lesson: Sponsors are a nice bonus, but they're not a plan.

options.text: Raise extra money and start building a hotel in space too
options.result: The space-hotel plans swallow the money long before your rockets fly regularly. Your shareholders are not happy.
options.lesson: Raise money for a clear plan, not just because people are offering it.

businesses.pitch: A big tropical water park with a wave pool, tall tube slides and a lazy river.
businesses.earns: Tickets and season passes, plus food, drinks, lockers, rented cabanas and tickets sold together with nearby hotels.
businesses.costs: Hundreds of summer staff and lifeguards, pumps and chemicals, huge water and power bills, slide checks and loan repayments.
businesses.risks: A rainy summer, a too-full hot day, dirty water, a safety scare, fake reviews and newer rival parks.
businesses.tip: Most of your money comes in a few summer months but costs run all year, so plan carefully and save for the quiet ones.

cases.title: The summer crew
cases.story: Your park opens in May. On a hot day 9,000 guests will come, so you need 300 summer workers, including 90 lifeguards. A staffing agency can send people next week for a 25% fee.

options.text: Hire in March, run a 3-week lifeguard course and pay a bonus to those who stay
options.result: The crew arrives trained, knows the slides by heart and stays until September. Few workers quit, so you hire and train far less in the middle of summer.
options.lesson: Training people early and rewarding those who stay costs less than constantly replacing them.

options.text: Pay a little more than other summer jobs so good people choose you
options.result: The best young workers choose your park, and the queue for jobs is long. Bills rise a little, but guests notice the friendlier team.
options.lesson: Fair pay is how you win the best people, and they win you the customers.

options.text: Make experienced head lifeguards team leaders, with a buddy for each newcomer
options.result: New workers learn fast from the buddies, and every slide has a leader. Mistakes get fixed quietly before a guest ever sees them.
options.lesson: Experienced people teaching new ones spreads good habits quickly.

options.text: Let the agency supply everyone: fast, but the fee is high
options.result: The workers arrive on time, but they leave for better jobs in July. You pay the fee again and again.
options.lesson: Agencies are fine for a rush, but it costs more than building your own team.

options.text: Hire a third fewer lifeguards at first and add more if it gets busy
options.result: The first hot Saturday has far too few lifeguards for the wave pool. Guests see it, the news hears about it, and you hire in a panic.
options.lesson: You cannot add lifeguards after something goes wrong: be ready before the crowd arrives.

cases.title: The cloudy lazy river
cases.story: After a record Saturday with 9,000 guests, the lazy river is cloudy and smells strong. You are nearly out of pool chemicals. A man in a van offers 30 unlabelled barrels at half price, cash today: 'Same stuff, the label fell off.'

options.text: Buy the cheap unlabelled barrels: half price, cash today
options.result: Nobody knows what is in the barrels. Hundreds of children go home with itchy eyes, the health office shuts the slides for a week and you refund tickets.
options.lesson: Never put something in the water if you cannot read the label and name the maker.

options.text: Close the river, test the water, order labelled chemicals from your supplier
options.result: Guests grumble for an afternoon, then read the test results on a board by the gate. By Sunday the water sparkles, and visitors post about how clean it is.
options.lesson: Close first, fix properly and show your proof: trust is worth one lost afternoon.

options.text: Sign a yearly deal with a licensed supplier that promises emergency deliveries
options.result: The supplier gives a lower price for a yearly order, and a van arrives within hours whenever you run low. You never panic-buy again.
options.lesson: A trusted supplier on a good contract is cheaper than a bargain in an emergency.

options.text: Fit sensors that test the water every ten minutes and alert the team
options.result: A sensor beeps on a Wednesday when the water drifts off. The team fixes it in minutes, before any guest notices.
options.lesson: Machines that watch all day catch small problems before they become big ones.

options.text: Pour in double the usual chemicals to clear the water fast
options.result: Too much chlorine makes eyes sting and skin itch, and guests leave coughing. The water still looks cloudy, and you used up the rest of your chemicals.
options.lesson: More is not safer: water care follows exact measurements, not guesses.

cases.title: Stars, hotels and a quick fix
cases.story: A new park across town has 4.8 stars online, and yours has 4.1. A marketing firm offers 500 five-star reviews for $4,000. A beach hotel group also wants to sell your tickets together with its rooms.

options.text: Buy 500 five-star reviews for $4,000 and catch up with the rival
options.result: A website spots reviews copied from other places and a newspaper reports on your fake stars. The consumer watchdog fines you, and real guests stop believing you.
options.lesson: Fake reviews trick your own future customers, and they do get found out.

options.text: Ask happy guests for honest reviews at the exit and answer angry ones kindly
options.result: A sign with a code at every exit brings in 2,000 real reviews. You answer the 2-star ones kindly, fix two slow queues and climb to 4.6 stars.
options.lesson: Honest reviews take longer, but they last and they show you what to fix.

options.text: Agree a hotel package, with a daily ticket limit so the park never overfills
options.result: Beach hotels sell your tickets with their rooms, and weekday visits jump. Capping the tickets means a hot Saturday never feels crowded.
options.lesson: Partners bring customers you could not reach alone, so agree limits and prices clearly.

options.text: Invite family bloggers for a free day and ask them to say it was a gift
options.result: Twenty families post about their day and say clearly that the visit was a gift. Bookings rise for a few weeks and then settle down.
options.lesson: It is fine to give away free visits, as long as you tell people what is a gift.

options.text: Cut all ticket prices by a third for the whole summer
options.result: More families come, but you earn less from each one and the rival cuts its prices too. Staff are busier and profits are smaller.
options.lesson: A rival can copy a price cut in a day, but it cannot copy being better.

businesses.pitch: A fun park with a carousel, a drop tower, a coaster, bumper cars and food stalls.
businesses.earns: Gate tickets and wristbands, season passes, food and drinks, games and party packages. Sunny summer days bring the biggest crowds.
businesses.costs: Ride staff, daily safety checks and repairs, electricity, insurance, and new rides to keep families coming back.
businesses.risks: Rainy or very hot weeks, a ride breaking down, a safety scare in the news, and a new rival park opening with bigger rides.
businesses.tip: Be clear about prices and strict about safety rules: families who feel treated fairly come back every summer.

cases.title: Wristbands and the fast pass
cases.story: Opening day is close. On busy days the queue for your coaster could last 90 minutes. A wristband for all rides could cost $32. You could also sell a Fast Pass that lets guests skip the queue, and families are asking about season passes.

options.text: One clear wristband price, plus a Fast Pass limited to 1 guest in 5
options.result: Everyone sees both prices on the website before they come. The Fast Pass brings in extra money, and the normal queue still moves, so nobody feels cheated.
options.lesson: Extra-fee options work when the price is clear and the normal ticket stays fair.

options.text: Sell cheaper early-bird season passes to local families
options.result: Hundreds of families buy passes before the gates even open. They come again and again, and spend on food each time.
options.lesson: Selling early gives you money and loyal guests before the season starts.

options.text: Build an app that tells guests when their turn is, so they wait in the shade
options.result: Guests play games and eat ice cream while they wait, instead of standing in a line. They spend more, and the queue complaints nearly stop.
options.lesson: A shorter wait feels better, and a happy guest with free time spends more.

options.text: Charge only $12 at the gate and make guests pay for each ride separately
options.result: Parents add up the ride prices and decide a day out costs too much. Many families choose the park down the road with one simple price.
options.lesson: If guests cannot guess what a day costs, they often stay at home.

options.text: Advertise 'Entry $15' and add ride, locker and Fast Pass fees at the very end
options.result: The low price brings crowds, then parents find a $60 bill at the end. The shoppers' watchdog is called, you refund the fees, and angry reviews pile up.
options.lesson: A price that hides its extras is a trick, and guests never forget it.

cases.title: The pushy dad at the drop tower
cases.story: Dev's son is seven and 8 cm too short for the drop tower. Dev is cross, says all his friends are going on it, and offers to sign a paper saying it's his own risk. Other families in the queue are watching.

options.text: Keep the rule kindly, and show them rides he can enjoy plus a grow-tall card
options.result: Dev grumbles, then the boy loves the bumper cars. The grow-tall card brings them back next summer, and a watching mum tells her friends how kindly it was done.
options.lesson: Say no to a risky request, then say yes to something safe.

options.text: Put a friendly height wall at the entrance so families know before they queue
options.result: Children measure themselves by a painted giraffe and choose rides that fit. Fewer families wait for 40 minutes only to be turned away.
options.lesson: Show a rule early and fewer people get upset about it later.

options.text: Teach ride crews to say no calmly, with a manager they can call at once
options.result: Next time a parent shouts, the crew member stays friendly and the manager arrives within minutes. Fewer arguments reach the queue.
options.lesson: Staff who feel backed up stay calm when guests do not.

options.text: Say 'rules are rules' and have security walk the family out of the park
options.result: The rule was right, but the way you handled it was not. Dev posts a video of the family leaving and the comments are unkind to your park.
options.lesson: You can be right and still handle a guest badly.

options.text: Let the boy ride, as long as Dev signs the paper
options.result: The safety inspector hears about it. A signed paper cannot undo a safety rule, so the tower closes for a week and you pay a fine.
options.lesson: A signature never makes an unsafe ride safe. Height rules protect the child, not just you.

cases.title: The sponsor with free lights
cases.story: Zing Drinks offers $400,000 a year for naming your main street, plus 5,000 free glowing lights for evening 'Glow Nights'. Its cheap electrician can start tonight and says there's no need for a licensed inspector.

options.text: Say yes, but a licensed electrician must fit and certify every light
options.result: Zing's money arrives, the inspector signs every cable, and Glow Nights make your park a late-evening favourite. Zing is happy to wait two weeks for a safe job.
options.lesson: Accept good money, but never let a sponsor's speed overrule your safety checks.

options.text: Ask two other companies for offers and pick the best partner
options.result: A phone company offers $520,000 and matching lights. Zing improves its offer too, and you choose the better deal for your park.
options.lesson: Compare offers before saying yes: the first deal is rarely the best.

options.text: Use the lights only at the gate and food area, far from cables and rides
options.result: The glowing gate looks wonderful and makes a great photo spot. The rides stay as they were, and your safety officer relaxes.
options.lesson: You can say yes to part of a deal and keep the risky part out.

options.text: Let your own handyman team fit the lights to save the electrician's fee
options.result: Two circuits trip on a damp evening, so Glow Night ends early. The insurer asks why a qualified electrician was not used.
options.lesson: Electrical work needs a qualified person, however handy your team is.

options.text: Accept the free lights and the cheap electrician: it's quick and costs nothing
options.result: On the first rainy night the lights spark near the drop tower and the whole park goes dark. The park closes for repairs, and Zing quietly walks away.
options.lesson: 'Free' becomes expensive if it skips safety checks near crowds.

businesses.pitch: A racing circuit with grandstands, pit garages, big race days and a kids' karting centre.
businesses.earns: Race-day tickets and parking, sponsors, TV deals, karting, and track-day fees paid by drivers, plus food and souvenirs.
businesses.costs: Safety barriers, marshals and medics, track surfaces, insurance, electricity, and the crews who run each event.
businesses.risks: An accident on track, rain cancelling race days, angry neighbours over the noise, sponsors who vanish, and costly repairs to the surface.
businesses.tip: Never trade safety for a big payday: a track trusted by drivers, fans and neighbours earns for decades.

cases.title: Barriers before the grandstand
cases.story: Your first race weekend is 10 weeks away and you have $1 million left. A 12,000-seat grandstand costs $700,000. Safety barriers, run-off areas and a trained marshal team cost about $800,000. Children keep asking about go-karts.

options.text: Pay for barriers, run-off areas and a certified marshal team first
options.result: The motor-sport inspectors give you the top licence. Drivers love a safe, tidy circuit, and top teams book your first weekend for their practice.
options.lesson: Safety comes first on a track, and it pays back in licences, drivers and trust.

options.text: Open a kids' karting experience with helmets, suits and trained instructors
options.result: Children queue to try karting at weekends, and parents watch from the café. It earns money long before the first big race.
options.lesson: A smaller activity can earn while the big project is still being built.

options.text: Build a first-aid centre and agree a fast-help plan with the local hospital
options.result: On race days a medic team waits trackside and the hospital knows the plan. Drivers and families feel safe because everything is ready.
options.lesson: Plan for the day you hope never happens, and people will trust you every other day.

options.text: Run track days for local drivers only, with no crowds, until all is ready
options.result: Track days earn a steady trickle of money and let your team practise. But without a big race you earn less and fans forget you exist.
options.lesson: Starting small is safe, but a business also needs customers who can find it.

options.text: Build the big grandstand first and add the barriers when ticket sales come in
options.result: Inspectors will not give a race licence without barriers. The grandstand sits empty for months while you wait for the money to finish the job.
options.lesson: Spend first on what you must have, then on what looks impressive.

cases.title: The quiet village letter
cases.story: People in the village 2 km away signed a letter. Engines are too loud on race days, and the council may stop evening races. Evening races bring in your biggest crowds, about $40,000 a night.

options.text: Meet the neighbours: 8 pm engine curfew, quiet weekdays, tree-covered banks
options.result: Some evening races move to afternoons, but the council drops its threat. The banks and trees mute the sound, and the village stops writing letters.
options.lesson: A fair compromise with neighbours protects your licence, and your future.

options.text: Give the village free tickets and a neighbours' day, and share race dates early
options.result: Families from the village come to the neighbours' day and meet the drivers. Several become regular fans and stop minding the noise.
options.lesson: People complain less about a place they feel part of.

options.text: Make every car pass a sound test at the gate and use quieter engine rules
options.result: A few very loud cars are turned away, and the rest get quieter. The village notices the change straight away.
options.lesson: Fixing the cause of a problem works better than apologising for it.

options.text: Tell them the track was here first and carry on as before
options.result: The council sets a 6 pm ban without asking you, and your biggest evening crowds disappear. The village is now your loudest critic.
options.lesson: If you refuse to talk, someone else will decide for you.

options.text: Cover the council's noise monitor on race days so the readings look low
options.result: An inspector finds the cover and a police report follows. The council fines you, evening races stop for a month, and every reading is now doubted.
options.lesson: Hiding a problem is never cheaper than fixing it, and it is dishonest.

cases.title: The Night Grand Prix offer
cases.story: SpeedKings, a race organiser, offers $3 million to hold a Night Grand Prix with TV cameras. It wants 30,000 seats (your safe limit is 20,000) and only half of the marshals, 'to save money'. It also wants seats on the run-off grass.

options.text: Hold it at the safe limit, every marshal post staffed, and share the TV money
options.result: SpeedKings grumbles, then agrees to the safe plan. 20,000 fans enjoy a smooth night, TV viewers see a tidy event, and you make a lot of money.
options.lesson: Say yes to the business and no to the unsafe parts. Negotiate, don't walk away.

options.text: Ask two tracks that worked with SpeedKings how the events went
options.result: One track says SpeedKings paid late and cut corners. You ask for part of the fee up front, and the deal is safer for you.
options.lesson: Ask others who have done business with a partner before you sign.

options.text: Tell your insurer and the motor-sport body, and get both to approve the plan
options.result: The insurer says a crowd of 30,000 would not be covered. With the extra approval, you are protected if anything goes wrong.
options.lesson: Check that your insurance covers what you plan to do, before you do it.

options.text: Say no to all big events: the track is not ready for TV
options.result: SpeedKings takes its event to a rival circuit and TV viewers watch it there. Your track stays safe, but nobody sees what you could do.
options.lesson: Playing it safe is good, but turning away every chance can cost you too.

options.text: Say yes to SpeedKings' plan exactly as written: 30,000 seats, half the marshals
options.result: The motor-sport body hears about it and cancels your licence before the event. Tickets are refunded, TV leaves, and the $3 million never arrives.
options.lesson: A big payday never excuses a plan that puts a crowd at risk.

businesses.pitch: A golf course with fairways, greens, a pond, a clubhouse, a cafe and a driving range.
businesses.earns: Yearly member fees, green fees from visitors, lessons, buggy hire, the cafe, the shop and the driving range.
businesses.costs: Greenkeepers, water and fertiliser for the grass, mowers and buggies, clubhouse staff, insurance and the loan on the land.
businesses.risks: A dry summer, a wet spell that closes the course, members leaving, a rival course, and tempting offers for your land.
businesses.tip: The land and the grass are your product: look after them, and think very long before you sell any of it.

cases.title: Members or pay-per-round?
cases.story: Your course opens next month. Members would pay $1,800 a year and play as often as they like; visitors would pay $60 a round. Weekends fill up but weekdays are quiet. How will you sell the course?

options.text: Offer both: yearly members plus pay-per-round, with cheaper weekday rounds
options.result: Members bring steady money in the quiet months, and visitors pay full price at weekends. The cheaper weekday rounds fill the empty mornings.
options.lesson: Two kinds of customer give you steady income and room to grow.

options.text: Start a junior and beginners' programme with the local schools
options.result: Children come after school, and their parents often join in. Some of those families become members when the juniors outgrow their lessons.
options.lesson: Teach children today and you are growing tomorrow's customers.

options.text: Open with half-price weekday rounds for the first month
options.result: Weekday mornings fill up, and many visitors return at the full price once they have enjoyed your greens.
options.lesson: A short offer lets people try you, as long as your normal price is fair too.
