options.text: Sell only yearly memberships: the money arrives at the start
options.result: The money is safe early, but passing visitors are turned away and the course feels like a closed club. Newcomers go elsewhere.
options.lesson: Steady money is good, but locking customers out limits how far you can grow.

options.text: Charge only $60 a round and hope the weekdays fill up
options.result: Weekends are busy, but weekdays stay empty. In every rainy week the income drops, with no steady money behind it.
options.lesson: Living on pay-per-round alone makes your income bounce up and down.

cases.title: A dry summer
cases.story: It is a hot, dry summer. The council asks everyone to use less water, and your water bill is $9,000 a month. The greens are turning yellow and members want green grass. A salesman has a cheap answer.

options.text: Water at night with moisture sensors, using recycled pond water
options.result: Sensors water only where the grass is thirsty, and night watering wastes less in the sun. The bill drops by a third and the greens stay healthy.
options.lesson: The green choice and the money-saving choice can be the same choice.

options.text: Let the rough turn brown but keep greens and fairways watered
options.result: A sign explains that the brown patches are saving water. Players understand, and the course saves money without hurting the game.
options.lesson: Save on what customers barely notice, and protect what they really care about.

options.text: Plant tougher grass on the edges that needs far less water
options.result: The new grass takes a season to settle, then stays green on half the water. Next summer the bill is lower and nobody frets.
options.lesson: A small investment now can lower your bills every summer after.

options.text: Buy a cheap 'miracle' spray that keeps grass green with no water
options.result: The spray washes into the pond and harms the fish and frogs. The council steps in and you pay for the clean-up.
options.lesson: If a product sounds too good to be true, find out what is in it before you use it.

options.text: Save money by cutting the greenkeepers' hours
options.result: Weeds creep in, bunkers go unraked and the greens turn bumpy. Members say the course looks tired, and some leave for the club down the road.
options.lesson: Skilled people make the course good: cut them and you cut your product.

cases.title: An offer for your land
cases.story: A developer offers $1.5 million for the four holes beside the road, to build flats. You would keep 14 holes. 'The offer ends on Friday,' says the developer. The contract is 60 pages long.

options.text: Get the land valued, then offer a 25-year lease on a small corner instead
options.result: The valuer says the road holes are worth far more than offered. The developer leases the car-park corner, you earn rent every year and keep all 18 holes.
options.lesson: Land is rare. Lease it or keep it, and sell only when the price and the plan are clearly right.

options.text: Sign on Friday: the cash is big and the developer is in a hurry
options.result: A hidden clause lets the developer build tall flats right beside your tees. Golfers complain about the noise and the dust, and the course loses its calm.
options.lesson: Pressure to sign by Friday is a warning: have someone you trust read every page first.

options.text: Add floodlit driving range bays for evening practice
options.result: The bays fill with office workers and families after work. Land you already own is now earning money every evening.
options.lesson: Make your land earn more before you even think about selling it.

options.text: Ask members and neighbours what they think before you decide
options.result: Members love the full 18 holes, and neighbours say flats would mean years of noisy building. Their views make your decision stronger.
options.lesson: The people who use your business often see what a big offer hides.

options.text: Sell the four holes and use the cash to pay off part of the loan
options.result: Members are upset about the smaller course and fewer visitors come. The loan is smaller, but so is the income that pays it.
options.lesson: Selling the thing that earns your money to pay a bill can leave you poorer.
